text: The Codex Arundel (British Library Arundel MS 263) is a bound collection of pages of notes written by Leonardo da Vinci, primarily between 1480 and 1518, and spans a 40-year period from 1478 to 1518. It consists of 283 paper leaves of various sizes, most measuring around 22 cm × 16 cm, with only a few being blank; two folios, 100 and 101, were incorrectly numbered twice. The codex contains short treatises, notes, and drawings on diverse subjects such as mechanics and the flight of birds, reflecting Leonardo's practice of using a single folio sheet for each subject, arranged as a cohesive treatise across both sides of the pages. Later book binders cut these folios into individual pages and stacked them, disrupting the original structure and creating a seemingly random arrangement. The manuscript is similar in format to the Codex Leicester, which also compiles notes, diagrams, and sketches, and is recognized as second in importance to the Codex Atlanticus. Written in Italy during the late 15th and early 16th centuries, most of the pages date from 1480 to 1518. The manuscript was acquired in the early 17th century by Thomas Howard, 2nd Earl of Arundel (1585–1646), and later presented to the Royal Society in 1667 by his grandson, Henry Howard, 6th Duke of Norfolk (1628–1684). It was first catalogued in 1681 by William Perry as a scientific and mathematical notebook. In 1831, the British Museum purchased it along with 549 other Arundel manuscripts (half of Arundel's collection) from the Royal Society; it was catalogued by the British Museum in 1834 and remained in the British Library as MS Arundel 263 after the library separated from the British Museum in 1973. The most recent facsimile was published in 1998, and on 30 January 2007, it was digitized along with the Codex Leicester as part of the British Library's "Turning the Pages" project and made available in the 2.0 format, reuniting the two Leonardo notebooks online.
